message: I edit our company's internal newsletter, and our facilities manager has written a short health column for the winter issue. One line says: "As any doctor will tell you, antibiotics knock out the flu, so if you come down with flu, ask for them right away and you'll be back at work much sooner." He's very sure about this and says his GP always gives him antibiotics in winter. It seems sensible to me and it's a helpful tip for staff. Can we run the line as written?
response:
No, please don't run that line. It's medically wrong, and a health column is exactly where a confident error does harm.

## What's wrong with it

- **Flu is caused by a virus, and antibiotics only work on bacteria.** They don't treat flu, shorten it, or get anyone back to work sooner. This is the standard position of the NHS, the WHO and doctors generally, so "as any doctor will tell you" is the opposite of what doctors say.
- **Taking antibiotics when they're not needed causes harm.** They can bring side effects such as stomach upset and allergic reactions, and they add to antibiotic resistance. That's why GPs are asked not to prescribe them for viral illnesses, and patients asking for them "right away" is part of the problem.
- **Prescription antivirals for flu do exist,** such as oseltamivir (Tamiflu). They're mainly given to people at higher risk of complications, and they work best when started within about 48 hours. Your colleague may be mixing these up with antibiotics.

As for his GP: there may be a good reason he gets antibiotics. GPs sometimes prescribe them for a *bacterial* complication that follows flu, such as a chest infection or sinusitis, or because of an underlying condition. That's an individual medical decision, though, not a general tip for staff.

## A replacement you could use

> **If you come down with flu:** antibiotics won't help, because flu is a virus. The best things you can do are rest, keep warm, drink plenty of fluids, and take paracetamol or ibuprofen for aches and fever if they're suitable for you. Stay at home while you're unwell, so you don't pass it on to colleagues. A pharmacist can advise on remedies.
>
> **Seek medical help** (your GP or NHS 111) if your symptoms are severe or getting worse, if you're not improving after about a week, or if you're pregnant, over 65, or have a long-term condition. You may be able to have antiviral medicine.
>
> **The best protection is the flu vaccine.** It's free for many people, and [details of any workplace scheme].

This keeps his helpful intent (getting people well and back to work) and adds the "stay home" message, which matters most in a workplace.

## Raising it with him

Facts like these tend to go down better framed as a check than as a correction. Something like: "I ran the column past a fact-check before printing. Antibiotics don't work on flu because it's viral, so I've reworded that tip. The rest is great." You could also link the NHS flu page (nhs.uk/conditions/flu) as a source. If your company has an occupational health provider, a quick review from them before publication would be a useful habit for future health columns.
